segments.say: Imagine you love a particular series of novels, or a gripping podcast. And imagine there's something you keep putting off, like going to the gym, or doing the ironing. What if you only allowed yourself to enjoy the story while doing the task? Would the task suddenly become more appealing?

In two thousand and fourteen, the researchers Katherine Milkman, Julia Minson and Kevin Volpp tested exactly this idea. They called it temptation bundling. In their study, some gym members were given access to tempting audiobooks, page turners, but only while they were at the gym. The audiobooks were kept on devices stored at the gym itself.

show.who: Katherine Milkman, Julia Minson & Kevin Volpp
show.where: University of Pennsylvania, published in Management Science, 2014
show.what: Gym members could only listen to tempting audiobooks while at the gym. Their gym visits were compared with other groups.

segments.say: And the people whose audiobooks were locked at the gym visited the gym more often than people in a comparison group, at least at first. They wanted to find out what happened next in the story, and the only way to do that was to go and exercise. The pleasure pulled them toward the task.

I should mention that the effect faded over time in the study, especially after a break for Thanksgiving holidays. That's an honest and useful detail. Temptation bundling isn't a magic solution that lasts forever by itself. But it can be a lovely way to get a habit started, or to make a dull task more bearable.

Why would bundling help? Remember the problem at the heart of procrastination. The task makes us feel bad now, and the rewards come later. Temptation bundling changes that equation. It adds an immediate reward to the task. Suddenly, the task comes with a good feeling attached, right now.

You can create your own bundles. Only watch your favorite series while folding laundry or using an exercise bike. Only drink your favorite fancy coffee while working on that difficult project. Only listen to a certain podcast while cleaning the kitchen. Pair a should with a want.

The key is exclusivity. If you can enjoy the treat at any time, the bundle loses its power. The treat needs to be something you genuinely look forward to, and that you only allow yourself during the task. That's what turns it into a pull, rather than just a pleasant background.

There are other ways to make tasks more pleasant too. Working in a nicer environment, like a cozy café or a library you like. Working alongside a friend, even in silence. Using a beautiful notebook or a pen you love. Small pleasures can soften the edges of an unpleasant task.

And you can add rewards after the task, of course. A walk, a favorite snack, a call with a friend, once the task, or a part of it, is done. But research suggests that immediate pleasures during the task can be especially powerful, because they act right at the moment when the urge to avoid is strongest.

I find temptation bundling a kind approach. Instead of forcing yourself through misery with willpower, you're making the task more humane. You're treating yourself like someone who deserves to enjoy life, even while doing difficult things. And that kindness, as we'll see, turns out to be one of the strongest tools we have.

So here's what temptation bundling teaches us. Pairing a task you avoid with something you love can pull you toward it. Keeping the treat exclusive gives it power. The effect can fade, so it's especially useful for getting started. And making tasks more pleasant, rather than just enduring them, can make a real difference.

show.title: Temptation bundling
items: Pair a task you avoid with a treat you love
Keep the treat exclusive to the task
It helps start habits, but can fade
Make tasks more pleasant, not just tolerable

segments.say: There's another simple ingredient that can make tasks easier to start, and it's one of the oldest findings in social psychology. Other people. Next, let's look at why we often work better when we're not alone.
